title: Miso Soup
subtitle: Japanese broth with white miso and mushrooms
excerpt: This is a light, clear broth that takes ten minutes from start to table. The miso must not boil after it is added -- boiling kills the beneficial bacteria and dulls the flavour. Traditional dashi is the base, but a mild vegetable stock works well as an accessible substitute.
sourceNotes: Miso soup is a foundational component of Japanese cuisine, served at almost every traditional meal from breakfast through to dinner. The base is typically dashi -- a stock made from kombu seaweed and dried bonito flakes -- but vegetable stock makes a workable substitute.

content.text: Never boil the soup after the miso is dissolved in. Keep the heat at a bare simmer and taste before adding salt -- white miso is already salty. This recipe uses vegetable stock in place of traditional dashi; the result is slightly less complex but the technique is identical.
Bring the vegetable stock to a simmer in the saucepan over medium heat. Add the sliced mushrooms and cook for 3-4 minutes until just tender.
Reduce the heat to very low. Ladle a small amount of the hot broth into a small bowl and dissolve the miso paste in it, stirring until smooth.
Pour the dissolved miso back into the saucepan. Stir gently and taste. Do not let the soup boil from this point on.
Ladle into bowls and top with the sliced spring onion. Serve immediately.

items.cause: Miso dissolved in too much liquid at once, losing intensity.
items.fix: Use less broth to dissolve the miso and add the concentrate to the pot. Also check the miso to stock ratio -- white miso is mild and may need an extra tablespoon.
